title: The Next Global Economic Crisis Could Be Made in China
gist: Michael Froman argues China's record-setting trade surplus and industrial overcapacity are approaching an arithmetic breaking point — the world can no longer absorb Chinese exports at current growth rates — and that without a coordinated, Plaza-Accord-style rebalancing, the resulting shock could rival 2008-09 while leaving Western governments with far less fiscal room to respond.

insights.claim: China's trade surplus reached nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025, growing three times faster than global goods trade, making it the largest trade surplus in recorded history.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: The pace of surplus growth relative to global trade growth is the key arithmetic tension the whole thesis rests on — a leading indicator of when absorption capacity runs out.
insights.quote: In 2025, it reached nearly $1.2 trillion, growing at three times the rate of global goods trade.

insights.claim: China now accounts for roughly 30 percent of global industrial production and is projected to reach 45 percent by 2030 according to a 2024 UN report, a concentration of industrial power with no historical precedent except the U.S. immediately after World War II.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: This is a structural, multi-year concentration of manufacturing capacity — relevant to any thesis on global industrial pricing power, deflation, and supply-chain de-risking flows.
insights.quote: China now accounts for roughly 30 percent of global industrial production, and by 2030, it is expected to reach 45 percent, according to a 2024 UN report.

insights.claim: China's current manufactured-goods trade surplus, measured as a share of global GDP, exceeds the combined surpluses of Germany and Japan at any point during the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Benchmarks China's current imbalance against the last major era of trade-surplus-driven friction (1980s Japan/Germany), suggesting today's adjustment pressure could be larger.

insights.claim: The core danger is arithmetic, not just political backlash: China's economy has grown too large to keep expanding exports at two to three times global GDP growth without eventually running out of customers.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Frames the entire piece's investment thesis — China's export-led growth model has a mathematical ceiling, not just a political one, meaning trade friction alone won't solve it.
insights.quote: Put simply, Beijing has outgrown its economic model.
insights.locator: Today, however, China has a much larger economy

insights.claim: The OECD estimates 60 percent of China's gains in global manufacturing market share have been driven by government subsidies, with state-directed credit access as the most significant implicit subsidy, letting firms expand without regard for profitability.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Quantifies the degree to which Chinese export competitiveness is policy-manufactured rather than market-driven, informing the case for countervailing tariffs.
insights.quote: The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development has estimated that 60 percent of China’s gains in global manufacturing market share have been driven by government subsidies.

insights.claim: Nearly 30 percent of Chinese industrial firms operate at a loss, up from 20 percent before COVID-19, rising to as high as 34 percent in sectors prioritized under the 'Made in China 2025' initiative.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: A rising share of loss-making firms in strategic sectors signals unsustainable capex and rising credit risk concentrated exactly where China is investing most heavily (EVs, solar, batteries).
insights.quote: Nearly 30 percent of Chinese industrial firms operate at a loss, up from 20 percent before the COVID-19 pandemic.

insights.claim: Local Chinese governments and state banks prop up unprofitable factories to preserve employment and tax revenue rather than allowing exits, producing a self-defeating price war that Chinese economists call neijuan, or 'involution.'
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Names the domestic mechanism (local-government-subsidized zombie firms) that keeps overcapacity building even as returns collapse — a structural feature to monitor via China local government debt data.
insights.locator: The Chinese word for this phenomenon is neijuan

insights.claim: A persistently undervalued renminbi combined with subsidies allows Chinese firms to charge up to 30 percent less than internationally based competitors.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Quantifies the pricing gap foreign manufacturers are competing against — directly relevant to margin pressure in autos, solar, batteries, and steel globally.
insights.locator: This system, in addition to a persistently undervalued renminbi

insights.claim: China is pursuing what economist Yasheng Huang calls an 'absolute advantage' economy, competing simultaneously with the United States in frontier sectors like AI and electric vehicles and with the world's poorest countries in low-value manufacturing like textiles — defying the standard comparative-advantage logic that led even South Korea and Taiwan to cede low-value manufacturing as wages rose.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Explains why China isn't naturally 'graduating' out of low-value manufacturing the way past export powers did, extending overcapacity pressure across both high- and low-value sectors simultaneously.
insights.quote: a country that competes simultaneously with the United States when it comes to artificial intelligence, electric vehicles, and electronics

insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Suggests rebalancing away from manufacturing toward consumption faces ideological resistance at the top, not just implementation friction — lowering the probability of a swift policy pivot.

insights.claim: Genuine economic rebalancing would require reconstructing the fiscal model every Chinese province and municipality depends on — land sales, subsidized industrial parks, and local financing vehicles — and accepting collapsed local revenues and mass layoffs, which local officials whose promotions hinge on growth targets have no incentive to pursue.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific political-economy mechanism (local government incentive structures) blocking reform, useful for judging how credible any future Chinese stimulus-with-reform announcement really is.
insights.locator: Local officials’ promotions are tied to hitting growth targets

insights.claim: German goods exports to China fell to their lowest level in a decade in 2025 — down 9.3 percent from 2024 and 23 percent from their 2022 peak — while Chinese imports into Germany rose by at least ten percent year-over-year across 2,241 product categories in the second quarter of 2025.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Quantifies the reversal of the German-China trade relationship, a leading indicator for EU protectionist policy shifts and European industrial employment stress.

insights.claim: German car exports to China fell 66 percent between 2022 and 2025 as China's total vehicle exports more than doubled and it became the world's largest auto exporter; Germany's metal and electrical engineering industry is shedding nearly 10,000 jobs a month, and Volkswagen is considering cutting up to 100,000 jobs and closing four German plants.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Direct, quantified evidence of Chinese overcapacity destroying jobs in a specific developed-market industry — auto sector employment and margin data in Germany is a concrete indicator to track.
insights.quote: Volkswagen is now considering whether to cut as many as 100,000 jobs—nearly a sixth of its workforce—and to end production at four plants in Germany.

insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Watch for EU Section-301-style tariff legislation as a near-term catalyst that could sharply raise costs for Chinese exporters into Europe.

insights.claim: After China demonstrated in 2025 its willingness to weaponize dominance in critical-minerals processing, the Trump administration convened the Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement, a multi-country coalition to rapidly scale 'China free' critical minerals supply chains — a template Froman sees for future coalitions closing markets to Chinese goods on the West's own timeline.

insights.so_what: Signals a coordinated Western critical-minerals diversification push as an investable theme independent of any single country's tariff policy.
insights.quote: Forum on Resource Geostrategic Engagement, convened by the Trump administration, is a coalition supported by dozens of countries, aimed at rapidly scaling public and private investment in “China free” critical minerals supply chains.

insights.claim: Unlike China's 2008-09 response — a roughly $586 billion stimulus (about 12 percent of GDP) that worked partly thanks to a growing middle class and expanding working-age population — China today has a working-age population that peaked in 2015 and an overall population declining since 2022, removing the demographic tailwinds that made investment-led stimulus effective last time.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: A repeat of 2008-style infrastructure stimulus is less likely to work this time, raising the odds Beijing has fewer effective tools if a demand shock hits.

insights.claim: When Chinese fixed-asset investment decelerated between 2012 and 2015, copper prices fell over 40 percent, oil over 60 percent, and iron ore over 70 percent, dragging sub-Saharan African GDP growth from 5.3 percent in 2013 to 1.3 percent in 2016; a full China demand shock today would hit even harder given deeper commodity dependence, since Australia, Brazil, and Chile send 25-40 percent of exports to China while Angola, the DRC, Mongolia, and the Republic of the Congo send 45-90 percent.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Direct, quantified precedent for how a Chinese demand slowdown transmits into commodity prices and emerging-market growth — a template for stress-testing commodity-exporter exposure today.

insights.claim: Froman argues a Chinese hard-landing could resemble 'Japan's lost decade — but worse,' since China's per-capita income (PPP-adjusted) is about half of Japan's 1991 level and a third of the United States' today, with a worse demographic outlook and none of the institutional recovery infrastructure Tokyo had.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: A useful downside framing: China entering a structural slowdown at a much lower income level than Japan did suggests a longer, harder adjustment with less policy space.
insights.quote: China could well face a version of Japan’s lost decade—but worse.
insights.locator: China could well face a version of Japan’s lost decade

insights.claim: Advanced economies now carry much higher public debt (around 110 percent of GDP) than they did entering 2008 (around 70 percent), while trust in U.S. crisis leadership has eroded — a February Politico poll found 42-57 percent of respondents in Canada, France, Germany, and the UK believe the U.S. 'cannot be depended upon in a crisis.'
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Higher sovereign debt loads globally mean less fiscal firepower to respond to a China-triggered shock than in 2008-09, and weaker U.S. leadership credibility could slow any coordinated response.
insights.quote: between 42 and 57 percent of respondents in Canada, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom agreed that the United States “cannot be depended upon in a crisis.”

insights.claim: Froman proposes a coordinated, Plaza-Accord-style rebalancing in which China commits to staged renminbi appreciation and phased-down subsidies alongside household-registration (hukou) reform, while trading partners coordinate the pace of their protectionism so the adjustment burden doesn't fall on any single economy or sector.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Lays out the specific coordinated-policy roadmap (renminbi revaluation, subsidy phase-down, hukou reform) investors should watch for as a signal the crisis risk is being managed proactively rather than left to blow up.

insights.claim: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has signaled Washington has largely given up pushing for comprehensive Chinese economic reform, instead pursuing narrower 'Board of Trade' purchase agreements on goods like soybeans, energy products, and airplanes — an approach Froman argues does little to reduce the broader overcapacity risk.
insights.speaker: Michael B. G. Froman
insights.so_what: Suggests current U.S. trade policy toward China is transactional rather than structural, meaning the underlying overcapacity risk Froman describes is not being addressed by present policy.
insights.quote: We’ve just come to terms with the fact that there’s not going to be some giant comprehensive reform of the way the Chinese political system works, including all these economic elements of it.
